analysis.one_liner: Strips federal protection from the lesser prairie chicken and blocks relisting for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill to remove federal protection for the lesser prairie chicken never advanced past its House committee referral, dying without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Interior Department had listed the lesser prairie chicken as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act, which restricts activities like oil and gas drilling, farming, and construction in the bird's grassland habitat in Oklahoma, Kansas, Texas, Colorado, and New Mexico. This bill would have erased that listing and barred the government from treating the bird as threatened or endangered before January 31, 2020, unless voluntary conservation efforts fell short of their goals. Interior would have had to report each year on progress under a state-led voluntary conservation plan and related agreements.
analysis.who_benefits: Energy and agricultural operators in the bird's five-state range. A threatened listing under the Endangered Species Act can restrict drilling, construction, fencing, farming, and grazing in habitat; removing it lifts those restrictions and the threat of federal enforcement or litigation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, wind, and ag operators in the range

how_it_helps.text: Removes the threatened-species listing outright, so any activity that would otherwise require a federal permit or be barred in habitat could proceed without ESA restrictions.

Blocks the species from being listed again before January 31, 2020, and after that only allows relisting if Interior publishes a finding that the voluntary Range-Wide Plan failed to meet its conservation goals — raising the bar for protection.

Relies entirely on voluntary conservation measures: the Western Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies' Range-Wide Plan, candidate conservation agreements, and state and private efforts, with annual monitoring reports to Congress instead of binding federal protections.

analysis.who_pays: The general public loses a legal safeguard for a grassland bird whose population had fallen sharply; conservation groups and wildlife agencies lose the ESA's enforcement teeth, leaving only voluntary, funded-by-participation conservation programs.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the Endangered Species Act's legal protections for a bird whose listing was based on a dramatic population decline, and relies on a voluntary plan whose goals may or may not be met; if the plan falls short, the public would have waited until 2020 for any federal backstop.

By statute, the Secretary could only relist after January 31, 2020 by publishing a determination that conservation has not achieved the Range-Wide Plan's goals — converting a science-based listing decision into one constrained by the statute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded a binding federal listing for a voluntary conservation plan plus annual reports. Energy and agricultural operators gain certainty and fewer permitting costs; the cost is that the only guarantee of the bird's recovery is a program without ESA enforcement, and any relisting after 2020 requires a new, higher legal hurdle.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Markwayne Mullin of Oklahoma introduced the bill on February 2, 2015, joined by ten House cosponsors, all Republicans from states in or near the bird's range.
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and the bill took no further action for the rest of the 114th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The lesser prairie chicken kept its ESA protections for the moment, since the bill died; oil, gas, wind, and farm interests in the range did not get the regulatory relief they sought from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The bird's federal protection stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Markwayne Mullin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the lesser prairie chicken's threatened-species listing.

for.name: 10 House cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors, all Republicans from Oklahoma, Kansas, Texas, Colorado, and New Mexico
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day of introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 2, 2015 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the 114th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 supporters (the sponsor and 10 cosponsors) were Republicans from the bird's range states; no Democrats supported it, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Oil and gas operators in the prairie chicken's five-state range
industries.note: A threatened listing can restrict drilling and related activity in habitat and expose operators to enforcement. The bill removes those restrictions, with the cost borne by the species' recovery prospects. The bill died, so the gain never happened.
Wind farms in the bird's habitat face ESA permitting and litigation risk; removing the listing clears that path. The bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Agriculture, ranching, and landowners in the range
industries.note: The listing can affect farming, fencing, and grazing practices in habitat and lowers land-use flexibility on private land; the bill would have lifted that pressure. It did not advance.

industries.industry: Voluntary conservation program administrators (Western Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies and state agencies)
industries.note: The bill designates the Range-Wide Plan and related agreements as the sole conservation channel and requires annual federal monitoring of them, raising their profile, but it does so by displacing the ESA listing rather than adding funding or mandates.
